pedagogy.summary: Estimating from a graph means reading a value the graph gives: an output y for a given input x, an approximate solution where a curve or line meets the x-axis or another graph, or a contextual quantity from a real-world graph. It is inherently APPROXIMATE — read to the nearest sensible interval, using the axis scale. It is best taught with an explicit 'up-and-across' reading routine, always stating the scale first, and treating crossing points (with the x-axis, or between two graphs) as solutions to be read and then checked.
bestPractices: Teach a consistent reading routine: find the given value on one axis, travel to the graph, then across to the other axis, drawing the path so it can be checked.
State the scale of each axis before reading, and read to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square — an estimate, not false precision.
Treat x-axis crossings as approximate solutions of 'f(x) = 0', and the intersection of two graphs as values satisfying both.
For a parabola, look for TWO crossings (or one, or none) rather than stopping at the first.
Sense-check every read-off value against the context — its units and a realistic range.
keyRepresentations: 'Up and across' reading lines drawn onto the graph
x-axis crossings as roots/solutions; intersection of two graphs as a common solution
Real-world axes (distance-time, cost) with a clearly labelled scale
A read-off shown as a band ('between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single false-precise figure
commonMisconceptions: Reads against the wrong scale (assumes each square is one unit) or reads off the wrong axis.
Gives a single false-precise value instead of an estimate to a sensible interval.
Stops at the first x-axis crossing, missing a parabola's second root.
Confuses where a single line crosses an AXIS with where two graphs intersect each other.

learn.summary: Learners estimate values from plotted linear and quadratic graphs using a consistent 'up-and-across' reading routine: state the axis scale first, find the given value on one axis, travel to the graph, then across to read the other axis. Reading is inherently approximate — report to a sensible interval, not false precision. Treat x-axis crossings as approximate solutions of f(x)=0 (a parabola has two, one, or none), and the intersection of two graphs as a value satisfying both. Real-world graphs (distance–time, cost) are read for contextual quantities with attention to units and realistic range.

activities.title: Up-and-across reading with the scale stated first
feedback: If read-off values are halved or doubled relative to the labelled axis, state the scale aloud and count grid units deliberately before reading.
If a learner writes 'y = 2' as if exact, or an over-precise 'y = 2.247', model reading a band: 'between 2 and 2.5, so about 2.25' — the goal is a sensible estimate.
Ask: 'If the axis went up in 2s instead of 1s, would your answer change? Why?' to surface scale-dependence.
activities.rationale: Misinterpreting the axis scale (not noticing the interval each grid line represents) is a documented graph-reading difficulty, and giving false-precise values is a commonly reported (though, in this row, unverified) error; an explicit scale-first routine and an estimate-as-band habit are proposed to target both directly.
sourceClaims: Reading values from a graph and misinterpreting the axis scale (failing to notice the interval each grid line represents) are documented student difficulties, and real-world (distance-time) graphs must be read for contextual quantities.
KS3 pupils should 'use linear and quadratic graphs to estimate values of y for given values of x and vice versa and to find approximate solutions of simultaneous linear equations'.
learnerActions: Before reading anything, state aloud what one grid square represents on each axis (e.g. 'each square is 1 unit' or 'each square is 2 units').
For a plotted curve, draw a line up from a given x-value to the curve, then across to the y-axis, and record the estimated y.
Read a value to the nearest sensible fraction of a grid square, writing it as a band (e.g. 'between 2 and 2.5, about 2.25') rather than a single over-precise figure.
Re-read the same physical point after the grid interval changes (e.g. squares now worth 2) and note how the number changes while the point does not.
activities.intendedInsight: A read-off value depends on the axis scale, so checking the scale comes before trusting any number; a value between grid lines is an estimate given to a sensible interval, not an exact figure.

activities.title: Finding both roots of a parabola
feedback: If a learner gives only one x for 'y = 0', point to the other branch — 'does the curve meet the x-axis anywhere else?' — and use the symmetry; scaffold rather than reteach.
If a learner answers 'y = 0' with −4 or (0, −4) (the y-intercept), clarify: 'y = 0 means the height is zero — where does the curve actually meet the x-axis?' and mark that axis.
For y = 5, check both symmetric branches are given (e.g. x ≈ 3 and x ≈ −3).
activities.rationale: Missing a parabola's second symmetric root and confusing axis crossings are reported errors (the supporting source is marked unverified in the row); explicit symmetry prompts and a y=0-versus-y-intercept distinction are proposed to address them.
sourceClaims: Missing a parabola's second (symmetric) root when reading solutions, and giving false-precise single values instead of estimates, are common graph-reading errors.
KS3 pupils should 'use linear and quadratic graphs to estimate values of y for given values of x and vice versa and to find approximate solutions of simultaneous linear equations'.
learnerActions: On a parabola such as y = x² − 4, find every x-value where the curve meets the x-axis (where height = 0), not just the first one encountered.

Use the symmetry of the curve: after finding one crossing, look on the opposite branch for its partner (a parabola that only touches the x-axis at its vertex has just one, and one that never reaches the x-axis has none).
Given a target height (e.g. y = 5), find both symmetric x-values that reach it, and read each as an estimate.
Distinguish 'y = 0' (where the curve meets the x-axis) from the y-intercept (where the curve meets the y-axis, here −4).
activities.intendedInsight: 'Find where y = 0' can have two answers for a parabola, located symmetrically; stopping at the first crossing misses a root, and the x-axis crossings are different from the y-intercept.

activities.title: Intersections as shared solutions, and checking read-offs
feedback: If a learner confuses an axis crossing with a graph–graph intersection, label each explicitly on the diagram and ask which question each answers.
Prompt: 'If I asked where this curve meets the line y = x, how would you find that from the graph?' then check the substitution.
For real-world graphs, ask whether the answer's units and magnitude are realistic for the situation.
activities.rationale: Treating an intersection as the common solution and checking a read-off against the equation (because poor scale or unlabelled axes yield wrong reads) are documented practices; real-world interpretation is a stated curriculum aim.
sourceClaims: The intersection of two plotted graphs is read as the solution satisfying both; an inaccurately plotted graph (poor scale, unlabelled axes) yields a wrong read-off, so a read solution should be checked (Mia's graphical sample response).

Reading values from a graph and misinterpreting the axis scale (failing to notice the interval each grid line represents) are documented student difficulties, and real-world (distance-time) graphs must be read for contextual quantities.
learnerActions: Read the intersection point of two plotted graphs (e.g. a curve and the line y = x) as the value(s) satisfying both.
Distinguish where a single line crosses an axis from where two graphs cross each other.

After reading a solution from a graph, substitute it back to check that it approximately satisfies the equation(s) (both sides come out close, not necessarily exactly equal), especially when the plot may be inaccurately drawn.
Interpret a real-world graph (e.g. distance–time) to answer a contextual question, stating units and sense-checking against a realistic range.
activities.intendedInsight: An intersection of two graphs gives the value(s) common to both; a graphical read-off is approximate and can be wrong if the plot is inaccurate, so solutions should be checked and sense-checked against context.

constraints: Report read-offs as estimates to a sensible interval (a band), not false-precise single values; the task is approximation using the axis scale.
State each axis scale before reading; do not assume one square equals one unit.

A static graph with pre-drawn read-off lines can demonstrate the routine but does not let the learner perform the reading across many different values, so pair any worked reference with active reading practice.

Recognition-only responses (e.g. multiple-choice on 'how many solutions') can check understanding of root count but do not by themselves elicit the learner drawing and executing the up-and-across reading; include tasks where the learner produces the reading lines and values.

An interactive draggable marker is one way to rehearse the routine and make dual roots salient; it is an optional scaffold, not a requirement — the same routine can be taught with pencil-and-paper reading lines on a printed graph.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session, and all activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source claim about missing a parabola's second root and false-precise values is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as a plausible but unconfirmed documented error (used in activities 1 and 2) and do not overstate its evidentiary strength.

The legacy row asserted '3D adds nothing' and that 'an open dialogue cannot rehearse the act of reading off a graph'; these are catalog-fit opinions, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened — reading plotted graphs is a planar task well served by 2D representations, while discussion can still support reasoning about scale, symmetry and checking, even though it does not itself execute the reading.
Self-audit of worked values for y = x² − 4: at x = 2.5, y = 2.25 (6.25 − 4), consistent with 'about 2.2–2.3'; y = 0 at x = ±2; y = 5 at x = ±3 (9 − 4). These are arithmetically correct and retained.

The KS3 claim supports both estimating y for a given x (activity 1) and reading x for a given y — including y = 0 roots and y = 5 — through its explicit 'and vice versa' wording, so its retention in activities 1 and 2 is on-principle, not merely topical.
The interactive 'live highlighting of crossing points' and 'scale toggle' are preserved as optional mechanism examples, not mandated features.

probeDeeper: You read y at x = 2.5. If the axis went up in 2s instead of 1s, would your answer change? Why?
You found x = 2 gives y = 0. Is there another x that also gives y = 0? How does the shape of the curve tell you?
How sure are you of that value — could you write it as a range rather than a single number?
If I asked you where this curve meets the line y = x, how would you find that from the graph?
assess.correctAnswer: (a) y ≈ 2.25 (read up from x = 2.5 to the curve, then across — about 2.2–2.3). (b) x = −2 AND x = 2 — both crossings of the x-axis. (c) x ≈ 3 and x ≈ −3 — the curve reaches height 5 on both branches. Values are read as estimates to a sensible interval, using the stated scale.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops at the first crossing, missing the second root ('y = 0 when x = 2')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Point to the other branch — 'does the curve sit on the x-axis anywhere else?' — and use the symmetry; scaffold rather than reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives only x = 2 for part (b), or only one x for part (c), ignoring the symmetric partner.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads against the wrong scale, treating each square as one unit when the axis says otherwise
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the scale aloud before each read and count grid units deliberately.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Read-off values are inconsistent with the labelled axis — e.g. halved or doubled.

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists on a single exact value, refusing to give an estimate or a range for a point between grid lines
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading a band ('between 2 and 2.5, so about 2.25'); the goal is a sensible estimate.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 'y = 2' as if exact, or an over-precise 'y = 2.247', ignoring that the reading lies between grid lines.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads off the wrong axis / crossing: for 'y = 0' gives the y-intercept (−4, where the curve meets the y-axis) instead of the x-axis crossings
errorPatterns.nextMove: Clarify 'y = 0 means the height is zero — where does the curve actually sit ON the x-axis?'; mark that axis.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers part (b) with −4 or (0, −4) rather than x = ±2.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot execute the up-and-across reading, reads the wrong axis, or ignores the scale; gives one root only.
responseLevels.full: Reads outputs to a sensible estimate on the correct scale, finds BOTH roots using symmetry, can read an intersection/solution, and states appropriate precision — transferring the reading routine to a new value and to an intersection of two graphs.
responseLevels.partial: Reads single output values correctly using the scale, but stops at one root or treats an estimate as exact — performs individual reads without coordinating symmetry or approximation across the whole task.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is the graph of y = x² − 4, drawn on axes where each square is one unit. Using the graph and showing your reading lines each time: (a) what is y when x = 2.5? (b) for which values of x is y = 0? (c) roughly what is x when y = 5?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Part (a) shows whether the child reads up-and-across on the correct scale; part (b) separates those who give BOTH roots from those who stop at one; part (c) exposes whether they recognise two symmetric x-values and offer an estimate rather than a false-precise number. Watching the reading lines, not asking about the method, is what reveals the procedure.
